headline: Fake GTA VI ISO circulates with malware; 113GB download is 99.99% empty zeroes with 50KB virus
summary: Internet sleuths confirm a massive 113GB GTA VI ISO file is fake, containing a 50KB virus designed to disable security software, padded with empty data.
details: A 113GB GTA VI ISO file is being shared online, but internet sleuths have confirmed it is entirely fake and contains a virus. The massive file is reportedly 99.99% empty junk data, with only a tiny 50KB virus embedded within.

Further analysis reveals the embedded malware attempts to whitelist the entire C:\ drive in Windows Defender and kill other security software. This poses a significant threat to users attempting to download the unreleased game.

The fake ISO capitalizes on the immense hype surrounding Grand Theft Auto VI, especially after recent gameplay and map leaks. Rockstar Games is set to release an extended look at the game on August 27, with the full release expected in November.

Bad actors are exploiting the high demand for the unreleased game to spread malicious software. Users are strongly advised against downloading pirated or unofficial software, particularly unreleased titles, as they are highly susceptible to malware.

headline_marked: [[Google lets users remove Gemini's visible watermark]], relying on hidden SynthID instead
headline: Google lets users remove Gemini's visible watermark, relying on hidden SynthID instead
summary: The easily removable visual watermark for Gemini-generated images can now be toggled off, as Google relies on a more resilient, pixel-level watermark called SynthID that's virtually impossible to strip out accidentally.
details: Google now allows users to disable the visual watermark on AI-generated images from Gemini Nano Banana models. This new "Media Watermark" option is rolling out in settings and might even be off by default for some users.

The visible Gemini logo watermark was easily removed using simple editing tools like Photoshop's generative fill, or dedicated reverse alpha-blending tools. Many users removed it for aesthetic reasons, not to hide the image's AI origin.

Google has long been integrating deeper protections, including C2PA cryptographically signed metadata. This open industry standard identifies an image's origin, whether from a camera or an AI tool, and is tamperproof but easily removed unintentionally by many editing apps.

The ultimate, more resilient watermark is Google's SynthID, woven directly into the image's pixels. Announced by DeepMind in 2023, SynthID is designed to withstand most practical image manipulations like filters, crops, and compression.

While not indestructible, SynthID requires deliberate, extreme manipulation (like cropping to 10% of original size or re-generating via another AI) to remove. Its strength lies in being virtually impossible to strip out by accident.

Google has a dedicated "SynthID Detector" portal, but it's currently in early access for media professionals. The article implies there's a simpler way to check, but the text cuts off before revealing it.
